hook: In a web browser, a tracked hand trembles and trails behind, and the usual cure for the trembling makes the trailing worse.
lede: Browsers now host far more than clicks and keystrokes: hand tracking through a webcam, physical tokens moved across an interactive table. When we brought these interactions into the browser, their data came out shakier and later than in native applications, which have direct access to hardware while web apps run in a sandbox on single-threaded JavaScript. FLOW is our lightweight answer: filter out the jitter, predict ahead to recover the delay, and do all of it in JavaScript with TensorFlow.js.

chapters.title: Smoothing the tremble lengthens the lag
paragraphs: Jitter and latency are more than cosmetic. Such instabilities have been found to affect users’ physiological indicators such as heart rate, and a gesture-controlled first-person shooter needs latency under 100 ms to satisfy its players.

The standard remedies trade one problem for the other. Moving averages smooth the data but add significant delay. The Kalman filter can also predict, but it demands many parameters, experience in signal processing and heavy matrix operations. The 1 euro filter, a low-pass filter whose cutoff adapts to speed, strikes a good balance; yet when browser latency is high, filtering can only partly relieve it.

chapters.title: Look ahead, and risk overshooting
paragraphs: FLOW treats every coordinate as a one-dimensional time series. A 1 euro filter first removes the visible jitter; it runs in constant time and fits in a few dozen lines of JavaScript. The filtered signal still lags, so a small LSTM predicts where the motion is heading, turning a window of past points into a sequence of future ones. Transformers are too heavy for the browser; this network has just two 140-cell layers and predicts in about 10 ms without GPU acceleration.

Prediction raises a new question: how far ahead to read. Latency is not fixed but varies within a range, such as 5 to 15 frames. Reading the prediction at an averaged, fixed frame eased the delay but caused significant jitter, especially as movements came to an end.

quote.text: After a high-speed movement comes to an end, the previous prediction methods we used often exhibit a noticeable “overshooting” effect, as if having inertia, departing from the actual position, and then bouncing back and forth like a ball towards the ground truth.

chapters.title: The filter knows when to brake
paragraphs: The fix came from inside the filter. Its smoothing coefficient α turned out to be highly sensitive to acceleration and deceleration, so FLOW maps α linearly onto the delay range and lets it decide how far ahead to read the prediction. A final 1 euro filter with default parameters then smooths out occasional stray points.

The interactive table shows why this matters. Tokens with metal contacts in a geometric pattern were recognized on a 55-inch capacitive touchscreen and sent to Chrome through a local UDP server, which adds latency, while a camera with OpenCV object tracking recorded where each token really was. Following Jota et al., we split movements into initial reaction, large ballistic motion and feedback-adjusted final adjustments. Prediction alone kept pace during fast motion but did worse than raw data in the final stage, where FLOW’s error was lowest (MSE):
points: Ballistic motion: raw 0.3215, 1 euro filter 0.2915, LSTM with a mean frame 0.0926, FLOW 0.0515
Final adjustment: raw 0.1817, 1 euro filter 0.1734, LSTM with a mean frame 0.1926, FLOW 0.0749

chapters.title: Steadier hands on every screen
paragraphs: Mediapipe Hands tracks 21 3D landmarks from a single RGB camera. GPU-accelerated Mediapipe served as ground truth for browser runs without GPU acceleration on a Lenovo Legion 7 Slim laptop, a MacBook Pro with M1, an iPhone 13 and an Android phone, each using its front camera, with test videos of volunteers aged 18 to 45. FLOW had the lowest error on every device and browser, below both raw and filter-only data, although differences between platforms remained.
Overshoot was less severe here than on the table, where system latency is greater. Next, we plan a browser-based table ice hockey game played with tokens on the interactive table.

takeaways: Filtering and prediction are complementary: one removes jitter, the other recovers the lag that filtering alone cannot.
A signal the filter already computes, its smoothing coefficient, can tell a predictor how far ahead to look and curb overshoot when motion stops.
Useful motion prediction can run inside the browser, in JavaScript, with a network small enough to spend about 10 ms per prediction.

facts.value: 2 LSTM layers × 140 cells (about 250K parameters for 30→15-frame prediction)
